doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Frank Tiberi, Basie's contrast and Caldonia contests
summary: Woody tells him to keep the pulse behind the saxes' laid-back phrasing, like Sonny Payne and Freddie Green with Basie.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Yeah. Woody’s band I mean — playing slowly, that’s it yeah — one of the first nights we played “Early Autumn” which obviously featured the saxes. And the lead tenor player, a great musician who is still with us, Frank Tiberi. Frank Tiberi would lay back so far on the beat it’d almost put you back a year. I mean he just [scats]. So one of these early nights I decided to go with the saxophones instead of keeping the pulse, I tried to phrase with them. And Woody goes, “No, no, no! Keep it up, keep it up!” All right? The only way, and I realized the only way that one gets the impression of them of the saxes laying back is if the rhythm section stays put, like the same idea with Basie. Those horns are laying back but Sonny Payne is back there on top of it like a son-of-a-gun.

And Freddie Green. Yeah. So you learn that contrast is an important part of the music, that everybody doesn’t necessarily have to play the same time. So learning that was good. I’ll never forget that. We’d have contests too to see how fast we could play “Caldonia.”
And Don Switzer, who was the bass trombonist on the band, had a stopwatch and he’d time the choruses. Oh man.
